Chapter 002
The Lantern Market

The lantern market opened an hour after sunset, when the brass trees along the river finally stopped ticking and the air smelled of oil and cinnamon.

Mira pulled her hood lower and slipped between two stalls selling copper birds that sang only when nobody was looking at them.

“You’re late,” said the old clockmaker.

“I’m exactly on time.”

“Then the time is late.”


ANTI-PIRACY: this story is published on another site; if you read it elsewhere it was taken without permission.

He handed her a small key wrapped in wax paper. It was warm, as if it had been sitting in someone’s pocket for a very long time, and it hummed faintly against her palm like a sleeping insect.

She did not ask what it opened. In the orchard, you learned early that questions had prices, and the clockmaker’s prices were never paid in coin.

Three gears for the gate, she reminded herself. One for the well, and one for the way back.

The crowd thickened near the fountain, where a juggler kept seven lanterns in the air without ever touching them. Children cheered. A guard yawned. Somewhere behind Mira, a bell rang twice, which meant the inspectors were coming down from the hill earlier than anyone had expected.

She tucked the key into her boot and walked, not ran, toward the river.
